q-10835:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{2}+8x.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+8x)=4x+8.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(2)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2)=4(2)+8=16\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=16$ and the coordinates of our point $(2,24),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(24) & =16(x-2) \\ y & =16x-32+24 \\ y & =16x-8.\end{aligned}
$$

q-24499:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=(\frac{3\pi }{5})$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{5})-{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{5}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{5}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{5}).\end{aligned}
$$

q-120348:
Our expression can be factored as follows:

$$
\sqrt{3}({cos}^{2}⁡{35}^{∘}-{sin}^{2}⁡{35}^{∘})
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x={35}^{∘}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡{35}^{∘}-{sin}^{2}⁡{35}^{∘} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot {35}^{∘})=\operatorname{cos}⁡{70}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}({cos}^{2}⁡{35}^{∘}-{sin}^{2}⁡{35}^{∘})=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡{70}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-120362:
Our expression can be factored as follows:

$$
\sqrt{2}(1-2{sin}^{2}⁡{55}^{∘})
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x={55}^{∘}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1-2{sin}^{2}⁡{55}^{∘} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot {55}^{∘})=\operatorname{cos}⁡{110}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2}(1-2{sin}^{2}⁡{55}^{∘}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡{110}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-139689:
Let's examine our diagram.

- There is $1$ arrow starting at Station A and ending at Station B. So, there is only one route from $A$ to $B,$ and so $a=1.$

- There is $1$ arrow starting at Station B and ending at Station B. So, there is only one route from $B$ to $B,$ and so $b=1.$

- There are no arrows starting at Station C and ending at Station A. So, there are no routes from $C$ to $A,$ and so $c=0.$

As a result, our route matrix is the following:

|  |  | To: |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **A** | **B** | **C** |
| From: | **A** | $1$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| **B** | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ |  |
| **C** | $0$ | $1$ | $0$ |  |

Therefore, 

$$
a+b+c=1+1+0=2.
$$

q-74762:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation, it must satisfy $T(kv)=kT(v).$ Noting that $[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 12\end{aligned}]=4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ 12\end{aligned}]) & =T(4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}])=4T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since we're told that 

$$
T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ 12\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 16\end{aligned}],
$$

we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}4T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]) & =[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\ T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]) & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\ T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]) & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-74775:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(kv+hw)=T(kv)+T(hw)=kT(v)+hT(w)\end{aligned}
$$

for any vectors $v$ and $w.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}T(3{v}_{1}+7{v}_{2}) & =3T({v}_{1})+7T({v}_{2}) \\ [\begin{aligned}13 \\ 5\end{aligned}] & =3T({v}_{1})+7[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ 3T({v}_{1}) & =[\begin{aligned}13 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ 3T({v}_{1}) & =[\begin{aligned}13 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\ 3T({v}_{1}) & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{1}) & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-74781:
First, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}37{v}_{1}+39{v}_{2} & =37{v}_{1}+37{v}_{2}+2{v}_{2} \\  & =37({v}_{1}+{v}_{2})+2{v}_{2} \\  & =37(0)+2{v}_{2} \\  & =2{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
T(37{v}_{1}+39{v}_{2})=T(2{v}_{2}).
$$

 

Now, since $T$ is a linear transformation, we have that $T(kv)=kT(v).$ So 

$$
\begin{aligned}T(2{v}_{2}) & =2T({v}_{2}) \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}21 \\ 17 \\ -14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}42 \\ 34 \\ -28\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, $T(37{v}_{1}+39{v}_{2})=[\begin{aligned}42 \\ 34 \\ -28\end{aligned}].$

q-12008:
A linear transformation $T$ satisfies two properties:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}]=kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}], \\  & T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}kx+ky \\ 4kx+3ky\end{aligned}] \\  & =k[\begin{aligned}x+y \\ 4x+3y\end{aligned}] \\  & =kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ 4({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+3({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{y}_{1} \\ 4{x}_{1}+3{y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{y}_{2} \\ 4{x}_{2}+3{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{T}$ is a linear transformation.

As a result, all three statements are true.
